text: I will leave out all discussion on republics, since I have already written about them at length elsewhere. Instead, I will focus entirely on principalities. Following the outline I mentioned earlier, I will discuss exactly how these principalities can be ruled and maintained.

I will say right now that it is much easier to hold onto a hereditary state, where the people are already used to the prince's family, than it is to hold onto a new state. To keep power, a hereditary prince simply needs to avoid breaking the customs of his ancestors. Beyond that, he just has to handle new situations carefully as they arise. As long as he does this, a prince with even average abilities will keep his state. The only way he will lose it is if some extraordinary, overwhelming force takes it from him. And even if he is deprived of his state, he will easily get it back the moment the usurper faces any serious trouble.

Take the Duke of Ferrara in Italy, for example. He never could have survived the attacks from the Venetians in 1484, or from Pope Julius in 1510, if his family had not been deeply established in that territory for a long time. A hereditary prince simply has fewer reasons and less need to upset his people. Because of this, he naturally earns more affection. As long as he avoids shocking vices that would make him hated, it makes sense that his subjects will naturally be well disposed toward him. When a ruler's power is ancient and long-lasting, the memories and reasons for wanting a change simply fade away. After all, one political change always leaves the foundation for the next one.
